data.title: The Clarity Act is stuck in the Senate: the SEC will first put US stocks on the blockchain.
data.description:
Recently, AMC CEO Adam Aron criticized Robinhood on X, claiming that the company had turned AMC stock into on-chain tokens without its consent, and that holders would not receive any shareholder rights. He used terms like "despicable" and "disgusting" to condemn this practice. Robinhood co-founder and CEO Vlad Tenev simply replied, "What's the problem?" The argument ended without a clear winner; both sides were simply stating their positions. On September 17th, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued a document that incorporated two unresolved issues from this dispute into its standards: tokenized stock must enjoy the same dividend and voting rights as the original stock; and any third party wishing to tokenize a publicly traded company's stock must first notify the issuer in writing, giving them a 30-day objection period. Aron has included the "consent right" it requested. The "shareholder rights" that users haven't received have also been established as a hard requirement. The standards have been set. The SEC's "innovation exemption" document is the most concrete statement from regulators on on-chain securities in recent years—not just a general statement, but a set of enforceable entry thresholds specifically designed to regulate "tokenized securities venues" operating within the United States. Robinhood Chain launched in June 2025 and expanded to include tokens of over 190 listed companies and ETFs in July 2026, covering more than 120 countries. These tokens, issued by Robinhood Assets, a Jersey-based entity, are essentially debt securities that only track stock prices. They are not offered to US users, and holders have no voting rights or dividend rights. This is precisely the product Aron criticized at the time.

Coincidence, not a judgment

However, a closer look at the jurisdiction reveals that this document and Robinhood's products are not actually under the same legal framework. The SEC regulates compliant exchanges within the US, while Robinhood Chain tokens were originally overseas products aimed at non-US users, and the SEC has not specifically commented on this dispute. The two lines align, or more accurately, it's a coincidence, not a judgment.

But even coincidences have their uses. This document, while not specifically addressing Robinhood, preemptively set the tone for this controversy—anyone attempting to replicate Robinhood's "tokenization without issuer consent" model will first run into this newly established standard. Tenev genuinely welcomed the exemption: Robinhood is striving to enter the compliant US market, and this standard represents a ticket to a new arena, not a constraint on its existing products. Who doesn't need to be regulated? SEC Commissioner Hester Peirce specifically clarified on the same day that this exemption was not intended for decentralized finance (DeFi). Her exact words were that truly permissionless smart contract-driven automated systems do not inherently pose intermediary risk and do not require an exemption. This statement was immediately retweeted by Uniswap founder Hayden Adams, who interpreted it as follows: Ordinary users trading in Uniswap's main pools are not subject to this exemption; what truly falls under the regulatory framework are the permissioned pools in Uniswap v4 that are targeted at specific groups and have entry barriers. The SEC's focus is never on "on-chain transactions" themselves, but rather on "who organizes transactions on-chain and who should be held responsible for them." This distinction differentiates Robinhood Chain's self-built, self-issued, and self-matching integrated model from Uniswap's open infrastructure—the latter being more easily categorized as a "compliance intermediary." This exemption also includes a separate clause for liquidity providers: institutional market makers who inject liquidity into these licensed pools using their own funds and provide quotes to clients can also be exempted from being classified as "dealers" requiring registration, provided they meet certain conditions. This means that market makers willing to cooperate with disclosure and record-keeping requirements can confidently place their funds into this system without worrying about identity verification issues blocking their entry. After the announcement, the prices of related tokens in several blockchain stocks rose, and UNI also surged at one point. The timing of this exemption is noteworthy. Just two days ago, the Senate only received 49 votes in the procedural vote on the Clarity Act for the U.S. digital asset market, failing to reach the 60 votes needed to advance, and the bill was temporarily stalled. However, the SEC did not wait for Congress. The exemption used its own administrative tools—a five-year term, conditional, and subject to adjustment based on feedback—without requiring new legislation. The CFTC chairman had previously stated that he was studying allowing existing exchanges to operate leveraged and margin trading under the "crypto asset market" designation, following the same line of thinking: a congressional blockade does not equate to a regulatory standstill; both agencies are pushing forward where they can utilize existing powers. The boundaries of this administrative path are also clear: for assets like stocks, which are already within the securities law system, moving holding records to the blockchain doesn't change their legal attributes, making it relatively easy for the SEC to regulate; however, designing a complete registration, custody, and auditing system for the entire digital commodities spot market still lacks congressional authorization. The exemption addresses the former, not the latter. The next step is to see who applies first. Another implication of this exemption is that it shifts the focus of the "stocks on the blockchain" issue from the narrative to infrastructure competition. On the same day, SEC Chairman Paul Atkins also held a roundtable discussion on 24-hour trading in the US stock market, focusing on the "23 x 5" clearing system already launched by the American Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC), overnight transaction information disclosure, and real-time inventory management—issues more fundamental than whether "tokens can rise": whether securities ownership and transaction records can be updated near real-time on the blockchain directly determines whether the US stock market can truly move towards 24/7 trading. For trading platforms, the next steps will be very specific: who will be the first to apply to become a tokenized securities venue (TSV) under the new rules, who will be the first to obtain written permission from a listed company, and whose smart contracts will be the first to pass the publicly auditable threshold. Whether this standard is effective depends on whether another company is willing to use it to measure others. Once the five-year period is up, the SEC says it will review the data to decide whether to convert it into a permanent rule. However, this document is ultimately an executive exemption, not congressional legislation—whether it will become a permanent rule after five years, or even whether it will be overturned due to a change in the next SEC chairman or a lawsuit, remains to be seen. Regarding on-chain stock trading, someone has finally spoken out openly about it, but who has the final say may have to wait and see for several more years.

data.title: Hong Kong's digital asset policy has shifted its focus.
data.description:
On September 16th, Hong Kong released its first Five-Year Plan since its return to China. In the over 100-page document, finance is defined as "Hong Kong's fundamental and greatest advantage," with three new areas highlighted: offshore RMB, gold, and digital assets. Most discussions focus on the conclusion that "Hong Kong needs to develop digital assets." However, if one only reads this level, they will miss the truly important change—the policy focus is shifting from "building markets" to "allowing markets to enter the financial system." This article will only discuss one thing: why this statement is important, who it will change, and what the next five years will look like.

01 In three years, Hong Kong has completed the "market establishment"

In October 2022, Hong Kong issued the "Policy Declaration on the Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong," which systematically set the tone for the first time; in June 2023, the licensing system for virtual asset trading platforms came into effect; in March 2024, the stablecoin issuer sandbox was launched; in 2025, the "Stablecoin Ordinance" was officially implemented, making Hong Kong one of the first regions in the world to establish a comprehensive licensing system for stablecoins.

In October 2022, Hong Kong issued the "Policy Declaration on the Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong," which systematically set the tone for the first time; in June 2023, the licensing system for virtual asset trading platforms came into effect; in March 2024, the stablecoin issuer sandbox was launched; in 2025, the "Stablecoin Ordinance" was officially implemented, and Hong Kong became one of the first regions in the world to establish a comprehensive licensing system for stablecoins.

01 In three years, Hong Kong has completed the "market establishment"

In October 2022, Hong Kong issued the "Policy Declaration on the Development of Virtual Assets in Hong Kong," which systematically set the tone for the first time; in June 2023, the licensing system for virtual asset trading platforms came into effect During the same period, "Fintech 2030" was released, with tokenization listed as one of the four key priorities; the Ensemble project entered pilot phase, and tokenized deposits began real-world transaction settlement; the GenA.I. Sandbox++ covered multiple sectors including banking, securities, and insurance; the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) approved secondary market trading of tokenized products; and the Hong Kong dollar stablecoin was launched in August 2026. In just over three years, licenses, sandboxes, legislation, and pilot programs were all in place. Hong Kong has essentially completed the task of "establishing a market."

02 The First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2026-2030) was released on September 16. For the first time, it clearly stated in an official medium- and long-term document that: in the next five years, we will promote the in-depth application of digital financial infrastructure, steadily and prudently promote the development of digital assets such as stablecoins, tokenized deposits, tokenized bonds, and tokenized securities, and expand the coverage of the financial regulatory sandbox.

02 The First Five-Year Plan for Economic and Social Development of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (2026-2030) was released in an official medium- and long-term document.

The plan also emphasizes adhering to the principles of "same business, same risk, same rules" to build a world-leading digital asset licensing and regulatory system, and to promote the practical application of tokenization technology through the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Ensemble project; in terms of the existing market, it will steadily promote the normalized issuance of government digital bonds. This marks the first time digital assets have entered Hong Kong's "five-year roadmap." The essence of the second half: "Let the market enter the financial system." The real weight of this statement lies in the second half. The policy focus is shifting from "establishing a market" to "letting the market enter the financial system." This isn't a difference in wording, but a choice of direction: digital assets are no longer an "alternative market" parallel to traditional finance, but rather to be embedded in the mainstream tracks of banking, bond markets, securities, and payment settlement—stablecoins will become the standardized settlement interface between the Hong Kong dollar, the RMB, and the on-chain economy; tokenized deposits will enter real bank transactions; tokenized bonds will be linked to the regular issuance of government debt; tokenized securities will move to the secondary market; and the regulatory sandbox will expand from a testing ground to a normalized system covering mainstream financial institutions. The inclusion of "same business, same risks, same rules" in the plan means that digital assets will no longer enjoy "special zone treatment," but will be regulated according to the same standards of mainstream finance.

04 Who Will Feel the Changes

For licensed institutions, tokenized deposits and tokenized securities mean new businesses, new balance sheet items, and also system upgrades and compliance investments; for stablecoin issuers, the positioning of stablecoins will be upgraded from "store of value" to "settlement tool," and whoever can first access the banking system and cross-border payments will gain a head start; for cross-border and RMB internationalization, the plan to promote offshore RMB and digital assets in parallel, and combinations such as RMB-denominated gold and RMB stablecoins are beginning to enter the realm of imagination; for investors, tokenized assets lower the transaction threshold and improve liquidity, but also bring new technological and market risks.

05 Four Indicators to Watch in the Next Five Years

Short-term (2026-2027): Stablecoin licenses will be issued regularly and "released from the box," with the first batch of application scenarios taking root; Ensemble projects will move towards more real-world settlements; and the regular issuance of government digital bonds will begin. Medium-term (2027-2029): The secondary market for tokenized securities will expand, tokenized deposits will scale up, and the sandbox will transform into regular rules. Long-term (2030): Digital assets are expected to become the infrastructure layer of Hong Kong's international financial center, and the regulatory system will become one of the global models.

However, uncertainties also exist: global regulatory disagreements, market volatility, cybersecurity and anti-money laundering pressures may all change the pace.

The word "prudent" itself reflects a clear understanding of risk. Next, we'll track four things: the number and application scenarios of stablecoin licenses, the secondary market liquidity of tokenized products, the "exit rate" of regulatory sandboxes, and the integration of offshore RMB and digital assets. To judge the next five years of Hong Kong's digital assets, don't look at slogans; these four indicators are enough. The market will gradually realize that this is not a short-term policy-driven rally, but a long-term project integrating traditional finance and blockchain technology. When real-world deposits, bonds, and securities are gradually tokenized, and stablecoins become standardized settlement tools, blockchain will truly transform from a concept into a fundamental technological component of the financial system.

data.title: The Federal Reserve resumes interest rate hikes: the end of an era of low interest rates.
data.description: Zhou Hao: For investors, this means that one of the most successful strategies of the past decade—betting on long-term interest rate declines and loose liquidity—may no longer be effective. By Zhou Hao, Chief Economist at GTJAI, a subsidiary of Guotai Haitong Securities. While the market was still immersed in the narrative of "interest rate cuts are inevitable" from the past few years, the Federal Reserve broke this conventional thinking with a 25-basis-point rate hike. On September 16, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. This is the first interest rate hike in over three years, and a formal reversal of the easing cycle expected in 2025. More noteworthy than the rate hike itself is the signal it sends: during the previous easing cycle, growth remained robust, employment remained strong, and inflation was far more sticky than the market anticipated; against this backdrop, not cutting rates, or even raising them, became almost inevitable. In this sense, the Federal Reserve is sending an important message to the market: the era of interest rates returning to pre-pandemic lows may not return. The most intriguing aspect of this meeting is the high degree of consistency between the policy statement and economic forecasts. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh explicitly stated that too many components of inflation have still risen by more than 3% in the past six months to a year. At the same time, the Federal Reserve raised its 2026 core PCE inflation forecast to 3.4% and its overall PCE inflation forecast to 3.7%. This means that after years of fighting inflation, price pressures have not completely disappeared. More importantly, the Federal Reserve did not lower its growth forecasts due to the interest rate hikes. Instead, the committee raised its GDP forecasts for 2026 and 2027 while lowering its unemployment rate forecast. This effectively breaks a core assumption in the traditional monetary policy framework: that interest rate hikes will significantly drag down the economy. At least in the Fed's view, the current US economy is much more resilient to interest rates than in the past. This is also the fundamental reason why the latest dot plot is so hawkish. Sixteen of the 18 policymakers expect further rate hikes this year, and four officials even believe that two more rate hikes are needed. More noteworthy is that the dot plot shows that the median interest rate will remain at 4.125% at the end of 2027, meaning that there is almost no room for rate cuts in the coming year. The market has historically viewed each rate hike as a prelude to the next rate cut, but the Federal Reserve now seems to want to break this conditioned reflex. To some extent, the Fed is undergoing a cognitive reshaping. For over a decade, investors have held a deep-seated belief that the Fed will eventually intervene to rescue the market should the economy slow even slightly. However, the Fed under Warsh has exhibited a drastically different style from its predecessors. Its record-breaking reduction in press conference time reflects its consistent advocacy for less forward guidance and lower policy communication frequency. In other words, the Fed is no longer willing to provide the market with a clear path forward, but rather wants the market to price in data rather than verbal promises from the central bank. This shift implies that financial market volatility may be higher in the long term than it has been in the past decade. The bond market has already begun to react. Following the meeting, the yield on the two-year U.S. Treasury note quickly rose to 4.74%, while the yield on the 10-year Treasury note climbed to 5%, reaching its highest level since 2007. For many investors, the 5% yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note is not just a number, but a dividing line of an era. In the past decade or so of ultra-low interest rates, the global asset pricing system has been built on the premise that the risk-free rate is close to zero. Whether it's the valuation of technology stocks, private equity financing, or real estate capitalization rates, all have benefited from extremely low discount rates. Now, this foundation is being completely rewritten. If the yield on long-term U.S. Treasury bonds can remain stable at around 5%, then many assets will have to be revalued. This is especially crucial for the stock market. This round of interest rate hikes did not occur on the eve of an economic recession, but rather in the middle of an economic expansion cycle. Historical experience shows that mid-cycle rate hikes are often more difficult to manage than those before a recession. This is because corporate profits have not yet deteriorated, but valuations have already begun to be squeezed by higher financing costs and discount rates. The two main forces supporting the rise in US stocks over the past two years were optimistic profit expectations brought about by artificial intelligence and market bets on future easing policies. Now, the second condition is weakening. If interest rates continue to rise while profit growth slows, then valuation expansion will be unsustainable. From this perspective, the real impact of the Fed's rate hikes on the stock market is not a slowdown in growth, but a revaluation of capital costs. At the same time, the US dollar has also received new support. Previously, as some economies in Europe and Japan gradually withdrew from ultra-loose policies, the interest rate differential between the US and other developed economies narrowed, putting pressure on the dollar index. However, as the Fed has turned hawkish again, the interest rate advantage has tilted back towards the dollar. For Asian markets, this could mean a new round of capital outflow pressure. Historical experience shows that once US real interest rates continue to rise, Asian currencies usually face depreciation pressure, and capital tends to flow back to dollar assets. The Japanese yen has become the most direct victim, and other Asian currencies are also finding it difficult to remain unaffected. For Hong Kong, the impact is even more direct. The linked exchange rate system dictates that Hong Kong must follow the US interest rate cycle. When expectations of US interest rate hikes rise, the interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar widens, carry trade activities increase, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate faces downward pressure. At the same time, local financing costs, the real estate market, and capital market valuations will continue to be affected. However, if this round of market turmoil is simply understood as a normal monetary policy adjustment, the complexity of the issue may be underestimated. In fact, the Federal Reserve appears so hawkish not only because current inflation data is high, but also because the US economy is undergoing a series of structural changes. First, the forces driving inflation are increasingly coming from the supply side. Neither geopolitical energy price fluctuations nor the expansion of capital expenditures triggered by investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure can easily suppress demand-driven inflation through traditional interest rate hikes. Second, the US fiscal situation is becoming a new macroeconomic constraint. Currently, the US fiscal deficit has long remained around 6% of GDP, and the federal debt continues to expand. The bond market is increasingly focused not only on the Fed's interest rates, but also on the US government's ability to continue financing in the future. In the past, the market generally believed that the risk premium for US Treasury bonds was close to zero. Now, this assumption is changing. The rise in the 10-year US Treasury yield to 5% reflects not only adjustments in short-term monetary policy expectations, but also a reassessment of the sustainability of US fiscal policy by investors. Secondly, the investment boom in artificial intelligence is reshaping the supply and demand relationship in the capital market. To build data centers, computing clusters, and energy infrastructure, large US technology companies are issuing long-term bonds on an unprecedented scale. This increased supply of corporate bonds is, in effect, competing with US Treasury bonds for global capital, pushing up the long-term level of the entire interest rate system. In other words, rising yields come not only from monetary policy but also from capital demand itself. This may mean that the central level of long-term US interest rates will be systematically higher than pre-pandemic levels in the coming years. Therefore, what is truly noteworthy in this round of interest rate hikes is not the widely discussed "how many more rate hikes there will be," but rather the Fed's redefinition of the neutral interest rate. The latest dot plot further raises the median long-term interest rate to 3.25%. This seemingly insignificant adjustment is actually of great significance. It signifies that policymakers are increasingly convinced that the natural interest rate in the US economy has shifted upward. Demographic changes, widening fiscal deficits, investment in energy transition, and the construction of artificial intelligence infrastructure are collectively driving capital demand to remain higher than in the past decade. If this assessment holds true, then global financial markets may be entering a new era: inflation will not return to pre-pandemic ultra-low levels, nor will interest rates. For investors, this means that one of the most successful strategies of the past decade—betting on long-term interest rate declines and loose liquidity—may no longer be effective. The Fed's 25 basis point rate hike appears on the surface to be a routine policy adjustment. However, at a deeper level, it marks a turning point. The US economy needs to adapt to higher financing costs, the US fiscal system faces stricter market constraints, global capital needs to reassess the attractiveness of dollar assets, and emerging markets must re-cope with the cyclical return of a "strong dollar." Therefore, the most important conclusion of this meeting was not that "the Federal Reserve has restarted interest rate hikes," but rather that the market has finally begun to realize that an era of low interest rates that has lasted for more than a decade may have truly come to an end.
